item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers drew six walks during Game 1 of the NLCS, including one from rookie sensation Josue De Paula in the top of the ninth inning.
De Paula pinch-hit for Kiké Hernández with the Dodgeres down 2-1, two outs, and a runner on first base. He drew a five-pitch walk against Milwaukee Brewers closer Trevor Megill, which prompted former Cincinnati Reds great and current NBC analyst Joey Votto to heap praise upon the Dodgers' 21-year-old-prospect.
"De Paula about to be in that upper tier quick, quick.," Votto wrote on X (formerly Twitter) during Sunday's game. In the comments of his tweet, the former MVP went on to mention De Paula's beautiful swing and elite swing-decisions.
The high-end comparison for De Paula has always been Yordan Alvarez, who the Dodgers famously once had in their pipeline. One can assume the likely 2026 AL MVP is certainly a player in Votto's so-called "upper tier" of hitters in MLB. De Paula didn't even swing the bat during his plate appearance in Game 1, but the seeds are being planted for what should be an incredibly successful career.
Dodgers' Josue De Paula is turning heads and could force tough managerial decisions in the playoffs
De Paula now has two walks in his three plate appearances during the postseason. His previous one came during the seventh inning of Game 4 of the NLDS, which allowed the Dodgers to score the go-ahead and game-winning runs to seal the series and advance to the NLCS.
Manager Dave Roberts could swap De Paula for the likes of Hernández, Tommy Edman, or Miguel Rojas. So far, during the postseason, the Dodgers are hitting .207/.282/.360/.642 in the postseason and De Paula's presence on the bench could help alleviate what has been an underwhelming postseason offensively for the reigning back-to-back World Series champions.
It takes every single player on the roster having a clutch moment for a team to win a World Series, and De Paula is showing that he is more than capable of providing an invaluable at bat if he is deployed properly.
De Paula's impressive, yet inconsequential, walk in Game 1 might already have Dodgers fans questioning Teoscar Hernandez's future this offseason. Unless De Paula can learn a new position on the fly like Mookie Betts, he'll completely blocked from the starting lineup by Hernandez, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, in 2027.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: Dodgers' three-peat dreams are on life support as the deflated heroes return home
item.dc:creator: Bill Plaschke
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - Bill Plaschke writes the Dodgers’ three-peat dreams are dying in the face of the potent Milwaukee Brewers. - The Dodgers’ aces have struggled to stay on the mound deep in games and key bats have gone silent. - After a humbling 7-4 loss in Game 2, the Dodgers need a miraculous rejuvenation at Dodger Stadium to extend their season. Once brimming with life, the Dodgers’ historic quest has curled up into a withered heap. The three-peat is dying. The three-pea
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
- Bill Plaschke writes the Dodgers’ three-peat dreams are dying in the face of the potent Milwaukee Brewers.
- The Dodgers’ aces have struggled to stay on the mound deep in games and key bats have gone silent.
- After a humbling 7-4 loss in Game 2, the Dodgers need a miraculous rejuvenation at Dodger Stadium to extend their season.
Once brimming with life, the Dodgers’ historic quest has curled up into a withered heap.
The three-peat is dying.
The three-peat is slowly, agonizingly having the life squeezed out of it by a collection of hardscrabble Midwesterners with no regard for stardom or status.
After two games of the National League Championship Series, the three-peat was formally been placed on life support Monday after the mighty Dodgers lost a second consecutive game to those little giants known as Milwaukee Brewers.
This time the final score was 7-4 after another devastating night at American Family Field, and now the Dodgers trail two-games-to-none in a best-of-seven series that appears beyond their control.
For a second consecutive game, their ace was knocked out. For a second consecutive game, their powerful offense petered out.
For a second consecutive game, they looked like a weary, aging band of fallen stars that had stumbled into a surprisingly deep pothole and had no idea how to climb out.
For the Dodgers to win this series and continue their journey toward a third consecutive championship, they must beat the Brewers in four of the next five games, the last two of which will be played in Milwaukee.
It doesn’t seem likely. It doesn’t even seem possible.
Not once in during their previous two title seasons did they trail anybody two-games- to-none, and they certainly don’t seem equipped to survive it now.
The Milwaukee Brewers dealt a blow to the Dodgers’ October psyche with their NLCS Game 1 win, but the Dodgers have shown they’re capable of bouncing back.
Look at how they lost on Monday. On second thought, don’t look, because what you’ll see bears scant resemblance to the swaggering, self-assured Dodgers of postseasons past.
They pitched their October ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and he’s always saved them, right? Not this time. He couldn’t make it out of the third inning, battered by scattered wildness and scathing swings.
They were handed runs on two errors by the Brewers shaky rookie starter Logan Henderson, and they’ve always capitalized, right? Not this time. They couldn’t make the Brewers pay for their clumsiness, managing just three total hits, the slumps of their superstars ever deepening, Will Smith and Shohei Ohtani now becoming absolute offensive liabilities.
Even with all this, they sent Henderson packing after four innings and took aim at a heavily used Brewer bullpen and surely they could summon the firepower to send at least one of those relievers running, right? Not this time, as four Brewer relievers set a major-league postseason record by pitching five perfect innings.
The last two innings being a sad microcosm of the previous seven.
Entering the eighth inning, the Dodgers only trailed 4-3 and had the top of their order coming up in what could have still been a trademark Dodger October comeback.
Not so fast.
Facing Abner Uribe, Mookie Betts struck out. Facing Aaron Ashby, Freddie Freeman struck out and Teoscar Hernández grounded out. Yeah, with perhaps their entire season on the line, they couldn’t even get the ball out of the infield.
The Brewers, of course, sealed the deal with two runs on three singles in the bottom of the eighth, and the Dodgers went meekly 1-2-3 in the ninth.
It was surely, truly painful for Dodger fans to witness the final out, a strikeout by … yep, last season’s World Series hero Miguel Rojas.
The three-peat is dying, and it’s almost unbearable to watch.
Having watched both of their top two aces beaten in Milwaukee, the Dodgers will now come home with Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow starting in Game 3 and 4.
In any other scenario, both pitchers are aces as well and the Dodgers would have a huge advantage. But neither pitcher has looked great in the postseason and both will be pitching while bearing the weight of a stressed-out Dodger nation..
What could possibly stand in the way of the Dodgers becoming just the third franchise to win three World Series in a row? Plenty, it turns out.
“Yeah, it’s certainly a challenge,” said manager Dave Roberts. “I think that, if you look Game 3, I like where we’re at as far as in a vacuum, who’s pitching, where our bullpen is at, being at home. Then you’ve got to go from there.”
Roberts still has hope. But he’s not looking past Game 3.
“As far as can we do it, absolutely, but it’s just you want to get that first one,” he said.
Dodger Stadium will be filled with fans in what could be a celebration. Or a wake.

item.title: [New York Post] Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith are zeros again in Dodgers’ devastating Game 2 NLCS loss
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris

item.content:encoded:
Heroes, zeros and other observations from the Dodgers’ 7–4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series:
Zero: The whole Dodgers’ offense –– but especially Shohei Ohtani and Will Smith
Really, the 7-4 scoreline in Monday’s Game 2 loss flattered the Dodgers. They managed just three hits. All of their scoring required the help of either a wild pitch or a throwing error from Brewers starter Logan Henderson. And once Milwaukee turned to the bullpen, their relievers retired all 15 batters they faced the rest of the way.
Still, as has been the case all postseason, it was Ohtani and Smith whose struggles once again loomed largest.
From the Nos. 4-5 spots of the order –– after Smith was bumped down from the three-hole pregame –– they combined to go 0-for-8 with three strikeouts. Overall in the playoffs now, Ohtani is 3-for-20 without any extra-base hits, while Smith is now an unthinkable 1-for-23 with one walk and eight strikeouts.
Even worse for Smith, Monday included a couple of regrettable moments from behind the plate.
In both the first and third innings, Yoshinobu Yamamoto threw what should have been called third strikes against Brice Turang. But both times home plate umpire Chris Segal missed the call –– and, most crucially, Smith elected against trying to challenge.
Manager Dave Roberts didn’t want to second-guess his catcher postgame, while Yamamoto also described both pitches as being “too fine a line on the [edge of the] strike zone” to challenge.
Still, both times, they missed ABS chances backfired, with Turang doubling and later scoring in the first, then walking and later scoring in the third.
“It was kind of early in the game, we kind of had him on the ropes,” Smith said, explaining his thought process. “I figured we could get him out there [without risking the challenges].”
Hero: The Brewers’ bullpen
The Brewers’ bullpen also figured to be one of their strengths in this series.
But two games in, their dominance has shifted the scales of the series.
In Game 1, four Brewers relievers (DL Hall, Abner Uribe, Aaron Ashby and Trevor Megill) combined for 4 ⅔ scoreless innings while working out of several jams with a one-run lead.
In Game 2, the group was even more dominant, with four arms (Dustin May, JoJo Romero and Uribe and Ashby again) going 15 up, 15 down over five perfect closing innings.
The Dodgers’ hope is that, as the series wears on, their lineup will benefit from repeated looks at the group. However, they will have to find some sort of answer to the unit’s premium stuff first.
As of Monday night, Roberts was still searching for one.
“I know that they’ve got good arms,” Roberts said. “But I think they’re just finding ways to win pitches better than we are.”
Unsung hero
Fifteen months ago, the Dodgers traded May away as an excess piece of their pitching staff.
On Monday, he was the one Brewers pitcher to inherit some danger out of the bullpen, but found a way to limit damage in what would prove to be the Dodgers’ final rally.
After Henderson’s second error of the game –– on an errant throw while fielding a bunt from Tommy Edman –– allowed a tying run to score and left Edman standing on second, May retired Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and Teoscar Hernández in order. Betts’ grounder did move Edman to third, while Freeman’s sacrifice fly got him home for a brief 4-3 lead.
But May’s performance set the tone for the rest of Milwaukee’s bullpen dominance.
And now, he could turn around and be available to start Game 4, in what would be his first outing back at Dodger Stadium since being shipped away by the team.
Key stat: Four
As in, the number of misses Yoshinobu Yamamoto generated from 33 Brewers swings.
The resulting 12% whiff rate was tied for the second-lowest of Yamamoto’s career. More consequentially, it stressed his pitch count and prompted his eventual early exit from the game, leaving too large a workload for the Dodgers’ bullpen (which gave up four runs in its 5 ⅓ innings of work) to withstand at a raucous American Family Field.
Quote of the night
“They had much better at-bats than we did across the board, top to bottom. And then they put the ball in play, created havoc. That’s what they do, and we didn’t do that.”
That was Roberts’ overall summation of the Dodgers’ Game 2 loss. It captured the many, but ultimately simple, reasons they find themselves facing a daunting two-game deficit as the series shifts back to Los Angeles for Game 3 on Wednesday night.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Yoshinobu Yamamoto chased early, Dodgers fall into two-game hole after Game 2 NLCS loss
item.dc:creator: Maddie Lee
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - Yoshinobu Yamamoto lasted just 2⅔ innings, and the Dodgers couldn’t hold multiple leads in a 7-4 loss to Milwaukee in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series. - The Brewers’ relievers shut down Los Angeles for the second straight game, putting the Dodgers in a 2-0 series hole as the NLCS shifts to Dodger Stadium. MILWAUKEE — Yoshinobu Yamamoto stood on the same mound where just a year ago he’d thrown a complete game and was pummeled by Brewers f
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
- Yoshinobu Yamamoto lasted just 2⅔ innings, and the Dodgers couldn’t hold multiple leads in a 7-4 loss to Milwaukee in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series.
- The Brewers’ relievers shut down Los Angeles for the second straight game, putting the Dodgers in a 2-0 series hole as the NLCS shifts to Dodger Stadium.
MILWAUKEE — Yoshinobu Yamamoto stood on the same mound where just a year ago he’d thrown a complete game and was pummeled by Brewers fans’ chants:
“Yel-li! Yel-li!”
This time, en route to the Dodgers’ 7-4 loss to Milwaukee on Monday in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series, Yamamoto had lasted only 2⅔ innings.
As American Family Field celebrated Brewers captain Christian Yelich’s two-run single for an early lead, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts emerged from the visiting dugout, ready to take the ball from the starter who’d made himself a household name with his postseason heroics.
Dodgers hitters are stymied by the Brewers bullpen, which throws five perfect innings in a 7-4 win that gives Milwaukee a 2-0 lead in the NLCS.
Yamamoto’s early exit put the onus on the Dodgers’ bullpen in a back-and-forth contest. And the Brewers’ bullpen shut down the Dodgers’ offense for the second straight game, pitching five hitless innings. The Dodgers finished with just three hits.
The NLCS heads to Los Angeles with the Brewers leading 2-0 in the best-of-seven series. The Dodgers will have home-field advantage for the next three games, needing to win four of the next five to return to the World Series.
It was the second straight highly touted pitching matchup, pitting Yamamoto against Logan Henderson, the Brewers’ 24-year-old budding star.
Yamamoto exited after giving up three runs and four hits in the shortest start of his career. Against Henderson, the Dodgers took advantage of mistakes by the Brewers’ usually fundamentally sound defense to score four runs against him, only two of which were earned.
The Dodgers’ offense started to chip away at Henderson right away. Leadoff hitter Mookie Betts worked a walk, which included a successful ABS challenge that turned a strikeout into a full count.
Betts then advanced to second on Freddie Freeman’s groundout to second and to third on a wild pitch.
The night before, Teoscar Hernández had zeroed in on the Dodgers’ at-bats with runners in scoring position in his postgame comments.
“We did a pretty good job,” he said after the Dodgers’ 2-1 loss in Game 1. “We just didn’t get the job done when we needed with guys in scoring position.”
His first at-bat Monday came with Betts 90 feet from home plate. Roberts had swapped Hernández and slumping Will Smith in the batting order, moving Hernández up to third and Smith down to fifth.
“For Teo to get three cracks at this guy, I like it,” Roberts said.
Right away, Hernández delivered. He fell into an 0-and-2 count but prolonged the at-bat and drove a fastball into right-center for a sacrifice fly.
The Brewers, however, evened the score without delay. Yamamoto struck out Jackson Chourio — whose leadoff home run last year was the lone run in Yamamoto’s NLCS complete game — to open the frame.
Then Brice Turang worked a full count and hit an opposite-field double. And William Contreras fought off a low slider, poking it into shallow left field to tie the score.
Two innings later, the Dodgers took the lead again, rewarded for hard contact as the Brewers’ defense showed its first signs of sloppy play. Tommy Edman led off with a single, and then Betts scorched a 100.9-mph one-hopper at shortstop Cooper Pratt, who mishandled it, giving Betts a single to put two runners on. Edman then advanced to third on a fly ball by Freeman.
Henderson tried to pick off Edman, but his errant throw gave the Dodgers the lead.
It didn’t last long.
In the bottom of the third, Yamamoto gave up a leadoff single and issued two walks before Yelich came up with two outs and drove a curveball into center field for two runs.
The first walk, to Turang, included a borderline ball four call. And the second, to Jake Bauers, came after 12 pitches.
As soon as Yamamoto left the game, it was clear it would be an uphill battle for the Dodgers.
The Dodgers retook the lead in the fifth with more help from the Brewers. After Kyle Tucker’s leadoff double, Edman laid down a sacrifice bunt. Henderson picked up the ball and sailed a throw to first, enabling the tying run to score.
Later in the inning, after former Dodger Dustin May replaced Henderson, Freeman hit a sacrifice fly, and Edman scored the go-ahead run.
This is postseason baseball, where the best pitchers take center stage and runs are at a premium. Would a stolen base or a sacrifice bunt every so often kill the Dodgers?
But, as had been the pattern all game, that 4-3 lead didn’t hold for long.
Roberts brought in left-hander Kris Bubic, replacing right-hander Roki Sasaki after a hitless inning, to face the left-handed-heavy heart of the order. But Bubic missed down the middle to the right-handed-hitting Contreras, who gave the fastball a ride over the center field wall, tying the score.
In the sixth, against Dodgers right-hander Brock Stewart, Contreras singled in the go-ahead run in a traffic-filled inning that included a Freeman error on a muffed pickoff attempt. Dodgers left-hander Tanner Scott came to the rescue and struck out Bauers and Yelich to end the inning, and Garrett Mitchell to kick off the seventh.
The Brewers added insurance runs in the eighth inning on RBI singles by Turang off hard-throwing right-hander Edgardo Henriquez and Bauers against left-hander Justin Wrobleski.

item.title: [Orange County Register] Dodgers shut out by Brewers’ bullpen again, fall behind 2-0 in NLCS
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE — Billboards around town promote the Milwaukee Brewers with the slogan “Win Our Way.”
The Dodgers tried. It didn’t work.
They scored four runs without getting a hit with a runner in scoring position – or hitting a home run. But the Brewers outhit them 12-3 and the final 15 Dodgers batters were retired in order as the Brewers pulled away to a 7-4 victory on Monday in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series.
“They pitched well and they hit good,” Freddie Freeman said. “That’s the name of the game, and they did it better than us today.”
They did it twice in Milwaukee. The best-of-seven series now heads back to Los Angeles with the Dodgers trailing 2-0. Game 3 is Wednesday at 5 p.m. with Blake Snell scheduled to start for the Dodgers.
“Grind. Win one game at a time, one pitch at a time,” Mookie Betts said. “The mindset can’t really change. We can’t add more pressure. There’s already enough as it is. Keep it simple. One pitch at a time. Figure out a way to get a hit.”
They have played hard to get for the Dodgers this postseason. Through six games against the Atlanta Braves and Brewers, they are batting .193 (37 for 192) as a team and, most costly, 2 for 26 (.077) with runners in scoring position.
“I don’t have an answer why,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I know that they’ve got good arms. So do we. I think they’re just finding ways to win pitches better than we are. Sometimes you’ve got to find a way to get a base hit and those guys — there’s a lot of balls that weren’t hit hard tonight but found the outfield grass. That’s hitting.”
The Dodgers found ways to score without hitting early in Game 2.
The pesky, opportunistic Dodgers scored a run in the first inning without a hit. Betts drew a leadoff walk, moved to second on Freddie Freeman’s slow roller then third on a wild pitch and scored on a sacrifice fly by Teoscar Hernandez.
They scored again on a pair of singles and a wild pickoff throw by Brewers starting pitcher Logan Henderson who was more effective throwing home than he was to first base.
That came up again in the fifth inning. Kyle Tucker led off with a double and Tommy Edman tried to bunt him to third – you wanted bunts. Henderson did him one better, fielding the ball and throwing wildly to first base. Tucker scored on Henderson’s second error and Edman wound up scoring on a close play at the plate (confirmed by replay) on a sacrifice fly by Freeman.
Each of the runs either gave the Dodgers the lead or tied the game as the two teams played in a phone booth, never straying more than a run apart.
That was true, in part, because Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto was not sharp. He threw 75 pitches to get just two outs into the third inning. The Brewers swung at 33 of those pitches and only missed four times.
“He wasn’t as precise as he normally is,” Dodgers catcher Will Smith said. “I thought they did a really good job, not expanding out of the zone, taking advantage, especially up the middle.”
Two key decisions by Smith could have changed things, though.
On a 2-and-2 pitch to Brice Turang in the first inning, Yamamoto seemed to hit the outside corner with a cutter for strike three – or he didn’t. That was the call by home plate umpire Chris Segal. It might have been overturned by ABS but Smith did not challenge.
Two pitches later, Turang doubled. William Contreras drove him in with a single.
“Yeah, I went back and looked,” Smith said of the questionable call. “I don’t know if it clipped it or whatever. It was kind of early in the game. We kind of had him on the ropes where we could just get him out there.
“The walk one was a bummer but I guess it happens. It’s baseball.”
That came two innings later. The Brewers had a runner at second with one out when Yamamoto again appeared to hit the outside corner with a splitter on a full count to Turang. Segal called it a ball and Yamamoto appeared to gesture towards Smith that he wanted to challenge. Smith didn’t.
“That one was a splitter. It actually cut back a little bit,” Smith said. “I just saw it out (of the strike zone) and didn’t know if it came back enough or not.”
Two batters later, Jake Bauers won a 12-pitch battle with Yamamoto – the longest plate appearance against Yamamoto this season – fouling off six consecutive pitches before drawing a walk to load the bases.
“I was trying to work on the edge of the zone,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter. “And some pitches it was really good but he just stayed on it. He did a good job.”
Two pitches later, Christian Yelich stroked a two-run single through the middle, the first base hit off of a Yamamoto curveball since August 27 and the last pitch Yamamoto would throw in the game.
“That changed the game,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said of Bauers’ walk, adding that he was told the confrontation lasted seven minutes. “You think about that and what it does to a pitcher. He can get through an inning in less than seven minutes and he does all the time. He’s one of the best pitchers in the land. It was a great at-bat. I think a turning point, I really do.”
It started the Dodgers’ bullpen turning.
Roberts turned to Alex Vesia to finish off the third and gave the ball to Roki Sasaki for a scoreless fourth.
But then he took it away from the converted starter after just one inning and gave it to Kris Bubic with two lefties coming up in the fifth. In between them was Contreras and he tied the game with a solo home run off Bubic. The Dodgers never regained a lead.
“For me, I felt Bubic had 4 out of 5 left-handed hitters (coming up), and that’s a perfect spot for him,” Roberts said. “I knew they weren’t going to hit for them. You have Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy — in my opinion, you’ve got a great spot for Bubic.
“That’s a decision I made, and we just didn’t — again, that’s his lane to be able to go out there and throw up a zero.”
The Brewers finally did things their way in the sixth inning against Brock Stewart.
He hit No. 9 hitter David Hamilton with a pitch. Hamilton went to second when Freeman mishandled a pickoff throw from Stewart and third on a ground out by Jackson Chourio. After an intentional walk of Turang, Contreras collected his third RBI of the game with a single to left field.
They did it again in the eighth against Edgardo Henriquez. Hamilton led off with a single, stole second and went to third on a ground out. Turang drove him in with an RBI single, giving the Brewers the first two-run lead for either team in this series. When Bauers drove in another run with a single, it gave the Brewers their first three-run lead this postseason.
Left to their own devices, the Dodgers couldn’t create another scoring opportunity. The final 15 batters went down in order against Brewers relievers Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby.
“They all throw 100 (mph) from different angles,” Freeman said.
The five perfect innings in relief are a postseason record. In winning the first two games of the NLCS, the Brewers’ bullpen has pitched 9⅔ scoreless innings.
“They attack hitters. They throw strikes. They’ve got good stuff, They throw hard,” Teoscar Hernandez said. “We just got to do a better job.
“I mean, they threw, the last two days, the same pitchers beside the starters. So we know what we’re gonna get during the games. They trust those guys. So that’s the guys that we’re gonna get.”
The Dodgers do not face elimination yet. But they must win two out of three at home in order to avoid it.
“We’ve got to find a way to get hits. That’s really it,” Betts repeated.
“They’re a really good ballclub. Really good arms. They’re swinging it. They’re playing really well. We have to come and be ready to go. There’s no secrets. We’re playing the game the same way. We’ve just got to find a way to get those hits.”

item.title: [New York Post] Brewers demoralize Dodgers, Yoshinobu Yamamoto to take stunning 2-0 NLCS lead

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE –– The Dodgers were hoping to hit the reset switch on Monday.
Instead, all they did was slam down on the panic button.
Losing Game 1 of this National League Championship Series rematch against the Milwaukee Brewers was one thing. Dropping Game 2 on Monday, however, threatened to put their season in suddenly dire straits.
This time, after all, they weren’t facing a presumptive Cy Young Award winner like Jacob Misiorowski. This time, more importantly, they had their own postseason stalwart, reigning World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto, on the hill to calm the waters.
But in a 7-4 defeat at American Family Field, an unexpected thing happened.
Yamamoto, despite entering with a five-game playoff win streak and the second-lowest postseason ERA in the last 100 years, couldn’t steady the two-time defending champions.
The Brewers, who allowed Yamamoto to throw a complete game against them on the very same mound in Game 2 of last year’s NLCS sweep, turned the tables decisively with long, relentless, unforgiving offensive rallies.
“They had much better at-bats than we did across the board, top to bottom, and then they put the ball in play, created havoc,” manager Dave Roberts said. “That’s what they do, and we didn’t do that. That’s the difference in the game … They did what needed to do tonight.”
Indeed, Yamamoto would last only 2 ⅔ innings in a 75-pitch grind against Milwaukee’s pesky, opportunistic offense. Despite being handed a pair of early one-run leads, he would depart the mound with the Dodgers behind.
It was a demoralizing turn of events –– keyed by a couple missed ABS challenge opportunities for Will Smith, an epic 12-pitch battle by Brewers slugger Jake Bauers, and a go-ahead two-run single from former MVP Christian Yelich that ultimately chased Yamamoto from the game.
While the contest would go back-and-forth from there, Yamamoto’s early exit gave the Dodgers’ bullpen too tall a task to withstand, sending the team back to Los Angeles for Game 3 on Wednesday desperately needing a response to a stunning two-games-to-none deficit.
“We got a lot of experience, we’ve been through everything before,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said. “So we’ll regroup tomorrow and go get ’em on Wednesday.”
The Dodgers did open the scoring Monday, manufacturing a first-inning run after Mookie Betts drew a leadoff walk, took second on a grounder, advanced to third on a wild pitch, then scored on a Teoscar Hernández sacrifice fly.
However, the Brewers responded with a rally of their own in the bottom of the first –– one that set the tone for their plan of attack against Yamamoto on Sunday.
With one out in the inning, Yamamoto seemed to freeze Brice Turang for a called third strike. But, home plate umpire Chris Segal inaccurately ruled it a ball, and Smith declined to use an ABS challenge behind the plate. Three pitches later, it would prove costly, with Turang getting a full-count fastball in the zone and slicing into left for a double. In the next at-bat, William Contreras came up and somehow stayed on a 2-2 slider less than a foot off the dirt, lofting a line drive just over Max Muncy’s head at third for an RBI single.
“It was kind of early in the game,” Smith said of the ABS decision. “We kind of had him on the ropes where we could just [try to] get him out there [even without the challenge].”
A similar story would play out in the third, as the Brewers erased a 2-1 lead the Dodgers took on an errant pickoff throw from Brewers starter Logan Henderson in the top half of the frame.
That inning began with a David Hamilton single. Then, after he stole second, Turang would again benefit from a missed ABS challenge opportunity –– with Smith declining to appeal another potential third strike in a full count, even as Yamamoto seemingly suggested he do so by pointing at his head himself on the mound.
“In that spot, Will didn’t feel like it was a strike,” Roberts said, trying not to secong-guess his catcher. “But obviously if you look back, [if] that’s a called third strike … that changes the outing.”
Once again, it set a disaster in motion. With an extra out to get, Yamamoto failed to complete the inning.
Instead, Bauers stepped up with two outs and forced Yamamoto into the longest plate appearance of his MLB career, drawing a walk from a grueling dozen-pitch battle.
After working a full-count, Bauers fouled off the next seven pitches he saw, chopping balls off the plate, to the backstop, into the seats, and –– twice –– just out of the reach of Dodgers fielders in foul territory.
The seven-minute duel went on so long, the battery in Yamamoto’s PitchCom device died after his 11th pitch, causing a delay while he was brought a replacement from the dugout.
“It just got to a certain point where it was straight compete mode,” Bauers said. “A little bit of a blackout, just kind of in the flow a little bit competing.”
Finally, on pitch No. 12, Bauers took a curveball in the dirt, loading the bases.
In the next at-bat, a clearly fatigued Yamamoto hung a curveball to Yelich, who lined his two-run single to center to give the Brewers a 3-2 lead.
That would be the end of Yamamoto’s day, marking the shortest outing of his playoff career. It would also leave too many innings for the Dodgers’ bullpen to cover –– even after the team retook the lead with a two-run rally in the fifth that was keyed by another throwing error from Henderson.
In the bottom of the fifth, Contreras greeted left-hander Kris Bubic with a towering game-tying home run that clanged off the bottom of the center-field scoreboard.
In the sixth, it would be Contreras again to push the Brewers back in front, lining a first-pitch single to left against Brock Stewart –– who had made his own mess by hitting a batter and firing an errant pickoff throw to first –– that gave the Brewers’ star catcher his third RBI of the day.
This time, the Dodgers wouldn’t have an answer, nor be gifted another pathway back into the game.
Rather, for a second-straight night, they were completely shut down by the Brewers’ bullpen, going 15 up, 15 down without a single baserunner after Henderson’s exit to finish the game with just three hits.
The Brewers, meanwhile, tacked on two insurance runs in the eighth, removing any pretense of late-game drama before a jubilant sell-out crowd.
Now, the Dodgers face a two-game hole they would have never imagined. Alarm bells are ringing. Their season, and World Series three-peat hopes, are dangerously close to being dashed.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Yoshinobu Yamamoto's postseason streak ends, Dodgers lose NLCS Game 2
item.dc:creator: Matthew Moreno
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers once again were the first team to score but they couldn’t hold a lead over the Milwaukee Brewers for a second consecutive night and now are facing a 2-0 deficit in the National League Championship Series. Other years the Dodgers trailed 1-0 in an NLCS but still won the pennant were 1988, 2018 and 2020. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers once again were the first team to score but they couldn’t hold a lead over the Milwaukee Brewers for a second consecutive night and now are facing a 2-0 deficit in the National League Championship Series.
Other years the Dodgers trailed 1-0 in an NLCS but still won the pennant were 1988, 2018 and 2020. Only in 2020 did they also lose Game 2, which was part of overcoming a 3-1 series deficit against the Atlanta Braves.
Brewers 7, Dodgers 4: key takeaways from NLCS Game 2
Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s short start
Yoshinobu Yamamoto took the mound a career 3-0 with a 1.23 ERA in his three starts following a Dodgers’ loss in the playoffs. He also had a streak of pitching at least six innings and allowing just one run or fewer in four consecutive postseason starts.
That was snapped as Yamamoto labored on Monday, completing just 2.2 innings and exiting with the Dodgers trailing 3-2. Yamamoto in particular had trouble putting batters away after getting to two strikes. One notable example was Jake Bauers fouling off six pitches in a row before earning a walk on the 12th pitch in the third inning.
Despite his uncharacteristic outing, Yamamoto became the third pitcher to start an LCS game in each of his first three seasons. He joined 1998-2001 Orlando Hernández (first four) and 1991-93 Juan Guzmán.
Missed ABS challenges
There were two instances where Will Smith or Yamamoto would have benefitted from initiating a challenge with the Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) system, and in both cases it came back to cost the Dodgers.
The first instance came on a 2-2 pitch to Brice Turang in the bottom of the first inning. It was called a ball despite catching the corner of the zone, and Turang doubled three pitches later. William Contreras’ RBI single then tied the game.
Turang was also batting in the third inning on another pitch that went in his favor. Yamamoto did appear to tap the side of his head, but was not convicted in doing so nor did he touch the top of his cap like players are instructed to. The walk put two on and the Brewers later loaded the bases before Christian Yelich delivered a two-run single that chased Yamamoto from the game.
Logan Henderson gifts runs to Dodgers
The Brewers, even if somewhat improbably, improved to 12-0 in Logan Henderson’s career home starts. He contributed to the Dodgers to manufacturing some offense in the first inning with a wild pitch allowing Mookie Betts to move to third base.
Teoscar Hernández’s sacrifice fly gave L.A. their initial lead. In the third inning, back-to-back singles by Betts and Tommy Edman put two on with nobody out, and the Dodgers scored the tying run on Henderson’s errant pickoff throw to first base.
Henderson committed another run-scoring throwing error after fielding Edman’s sacrifice bunt attempt.
That marked the end of the road for the Brewers’ rookie at four-plus innings pitched and four runs (two earned) allowed.
William Contreras powers Brewers
Milwaukee was carried by Contreras leading all players with xx RBI. Building off his RBI single in the first inning, Contreras tied the game again in the fifth on a solo home run off Kris Bubic.
Then after an intentional walk put runners at the corners with one out in the sixth inning, Contreras pulled an RBI single into left field that gave the Brewers their decided lead.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Roberts Calls Yoshinobu Yamamoto's Preparation "Spectacular"
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: MILWAUKEE, WI — Dave Roberts has watched Yoshinobu Yamamoto prepare for enough big starts to know how much work goes into his calm on the mound. Before Monday’s Game 2 in Milwaukee, Roberts called that preparation “spectacular” and compared his care for each detail with Clayton Kershaw’s. item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE, WI — Dave Roberts has watched Yoshinobu Yamamoto prepare for enough big starts to know how much work goes into his calm on the mound. Before Monday’s Game 2 in Milwaukee, Roberts called that preparation “spectacular” and compared his care for each detail with Clayton Kershaw’s. With the Dodgers trailing the series 1–0, Yamamoto gets the ball against Logan Henderson. Roberts also made a change to the batting order, moving Teoscar Hernández up and Will Smith to fifth.
“Everything he does is for a purpose”
Asked what helps Yamamoto thrive in big moments, Roberts began with the person behind the pitches.
“Part of it is who he is, as far as his makeup, his toughness, the work ethic, the culture piece of it,” Roberts said. “Everything he does is for a purpose, really. When you work and prepare the way he does, I’ve never seen anyone prepare like him. No one.”
“When you take it into a game, that’s why he is so unflappable and continues to make pitches when he needs to. Obviously, the pitch mix is next level. The delivery is next level. He has pitches to get left and right out. The command is next level.”
Roberts sees that work as a foundation for how Yamamoto handles pressure.
“The moment never gets too big. He manages his heartbeat,” he said. “I had Clayton Kershaw for 10 years, and no one did it like him until Yamamoto, in the sense of every single thing he does and what it takes to prepare for a day. It’s spectacular.”
Teoscar moves up, Smith hits fifth
Roberts moved Smith down two spots, giving Hernández an earlier turn against Henderson’s fastball, changeup and cutter.
“With this pitcher in particular, I like Teo. For Teo to get three cracks at this guy, I like it,” Roberts said. “Teo’s swinging well. But that five spot, as we talked about in the DS, the game falls to the five spot a lot.”
“Will’s going to have a chance to get a couple two-out hits that can change the game. Moving down two spots, but it’s still a very, very important spot.”
Smith said earlier that his swing feels better than his results. Roberts has seen signs of that, too.
“The last couple games, it’s been better. He still takes a good at-bat. It just hasn’t lined up yet,” Roberts said. “In this moment in time, everything rightfully is more magnified. It’s five games. All it takes is squaring one ball up, and it flips.”
“I still trust him in the batter’s box.”
A different test against Henderson
The Dodgers expect a different challenge from Henderson than they faced against Jacob Misiorowski in the opener.
“Good young pitcher. We’ve seen him a couple times,” Roberts said. “It’s a really good fastball that plays up with the characteristics, low slot. He’s got a good changeup that runs, misses the bat. Good versus right and left, and a good athlete.”
“It’s going to be a tough battle. It’s going to be a different approach than a Misiorowski kind of thing. He’s really good. Very, very good young pitcher.”
Roberts liked the work of his lineup Sunday. Now he wants more of those at-bats to end with hits.
“I like the intent, one through nine. I like the fight, seeing pitches, winning pitches,” he said. “Now it gets to finishing off the at-bat with some hits, hitting some outfield grass and trying to get more line drives versus the fly balls.”
“I think that’s inches, centimeters. I’ll bet on how we go about taking at-bats to then expect a good result. We’ve got to go out there with the same intent, and then we’ll put up some runs.”
Taking their shots
Roberts believes the Dodgers can use their power against Henderson while still finding ways to move runners and bring them home.
“We’re built to slug. Henderson’s a heck of a pitcher, but we’ve got to be able to take some shots and see if we can knock the ball out of the ballpark,” he said.
“You still need to take those at-bats and be able to get a base hit, hit behind a runner, like Andy did yesterday to drive in a run. That’s baseball.”
“As far as the bunt, the hit-and-run, stuff like that, you also have to have the right personnel.”

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers look to even up the NLCS in Game 2 against the Milwaukee Brewers. Last night, they fell 0-1 in the series after a 2-1 pitching duel.
The Dodgers offense was nearly nonexistent, leaving nine runners on base and going 1-for-6 with RISP.
In today’s 2:00 P.M. PST game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made a lineup change involving their best postseason hitter.
Kiké Hernández Out, Tommy Edman In vs. Brewers
Per Los Angeles Dodgers reporter David Vassegh, Kiké Hernández will sit tonight with Tommy Edman taking his place at second and batting ninth.
In five games this postseason, Edman has yet to record hit.
In Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves, Hernández hit a towering two-run home run ultimately lifting the Dodgers to victory.
Aside from that home run, both Edman and Hernández’s bats have been awfully quiet.
But, the NLCS is where Edman shines. In 2024, he won NLCS MVP. Recording 11 RBIS–tying a franchise record–with a home run, and a .407 batting average which included a hit in each game.
Last year against Milwakuee in the NLCS, Edman tallied five hits and three RBIs.
Tonight, the Dodgers need at least one bat to breakout and shift the momentum of the series before heading home for Games 3 through 5.

Dave Roberts made several slight tweaks aside from the Tommy Edman, Kiké Hernández switch.

Tucker has occupied that lower spot throughout the postse
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers released their lineup for Game 1 of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers on Sunday, and the placement of Kyle Tucker once again drew attention.
Manager Dave Roberts slotted the outfielder eighth in the order despite the presence of right-hander Jacob Misiorowski on the mound for Milwaukee, a matchup that might otherwise favor a left-handed bat higher in the lineup, via Underdog MLB.
Tucker has occupied that lower spot throughout the postseason, including during the Dodgers’ series against the Atlanta Braves.
The decision keeps him in right field while the top of the order features Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freddie Freeman at first base, Will Smith catching, and Shohei Ohtani as the designated hitter batting cleanup. Teoscar Hernández, Max Muncy, and Andy Pages follow before Tucker, with Enrique Hernández handling second base in place of the unavailable Tommy Edman and Miguel Rojas.
Tarik Skubal, acquired from Detroit at the trade deadline, starts for Los Angeles opposite Misiorowski in the series opener at American Family Field.
The arrangement reflects a broader pattern for Tucker in his first season with the Dodgers. After signing a four-year, $240 million contract in free agency, choosing the defending champions over longer offers elsewhere, he posted a .233 batting average with 17 home runs and 70 RBIs across 154 regular-season games.
Those numbers fell short of the production many expected from a player who had delivered multiple 30-home-run seasons earlier in his career. Roberts and the front office have nonetheless kept him in the everyday mix, banking on the October performance that motivated the signing in the first place.
Tucker has shown signs of that form since early September and carried it into the Division Series. He went 5-for-15 with a home run, two RBIs, and two stolen bases against Atlanta, batting .333 in limited action.
Those at-bats included a two-run homer in the series opener at Dodger Stadium.
With the Dodgers seeking a third consecutive World Series appearance, the NLCS against a Brewers club that won 103 games offers the clearest stage yet for the 29-year-old to justify the investment.
A productive stretch against Milwaukee’s pitching staff would quiet questions about his regular-season output and reinforce the club’s bet that his best baseball remains ahead.
For now, the eighth spot keeps Tucker in the lineup without disrupting the balance Roberts has settled on for the series.
Both clubs enter the matchup after efficient Division Series victories, and the early pitching duel between Skubal and Misiorowski sets a high bar for the hitters behind them.
Tucker’s ability to contribute from the lower third of the order will factor into whether Los Angeles can seize an early advantage on the road.

item.title: [New York Post] How the ‘Dinosaur’ Dodgers continue to find the fountain of youth
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: MILWAUKEE –– Dave Roberts delivered the speech. Teoscar Hernández supplied the punch line. In the wake of their National League Division Series defeat of the Atlanta Braves last week, the Dodgers gathered around their manager at the start of a champagne celebration in Truist Park’s visiting clubhouse. First, Roberts extolled their culture and competitiveness. He then declared that “we’re smarter, we’re better and we’re tougher” than their postseason competition. That’s when, from the corner of t
item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE –– Dave Roberts delivered the speech. Teoscar Hernández supplied the punch line.
In the wake of their National League Division Series defeat of the Atlanta Braves last week, the Dodgers gathered around their manager at the start of a champagne celebration in Truist Park’s visiting clubhouse.
First, Roberts extolled their culture and competitiveness. He then declared that “we’re smarter, we’re better and we’re tougher” than their postseason competition.
That’s when, from the corner of the room, Hernández chimed in with one more observation.
“And we’re dinosaurs!” he shouted.
Cretaceous creatures, who have once again found the fountain of October youth.
Throughout the regular season and leading into the playoffs, the Dodgers’ aging roster loomed as their biggest area of concern. Their average lineup age of 30.9 years old, according to Baseball Reference, was the oldest in the majors.
Their grizzled veteran core has played more games (and traveled more miles, including two season-opening Asia trips) than any other club in baseball the past two years.

California Post Newsletters: Sign up here!
California Post App: Download here!
Home delivery: Sign up here!
Page Six Hollywood: Sign up here!
That’s why the team could help but notice the recent “dinosaur” comment made by new Padres owner José E. Feliciano –– even if he was trying to refer to the actual collection of fossils kept by Dodgers owner Mark Walter.
To the two-time defending champions, it still qualified as a perceived slight.
“We’ve heard it,” 36-year-old third baseman Max Muncy said. “But you can’t focus on the outside stuff for us.
Indeed, the Dodgers do not need any extra motivation this postseason, as they continue their quest for a third-straight World Series title in the NL Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
“You worry about yourself,” Muncy said. “You worry about how you’re getting ready for the game, how you’re preparing for the series.”
But talk about their age has nonetheless added some fuel to their competitive fire.
“Los Viejitos!!!” Kiké Hernández captioned on an Instagram photo of him, Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Mookie Betts and Freddie Freeman earlier this week –– playfully using the Spanish term for “old folks” to describe the club’s five eldest statesmen.
“I like our dinosaurs,” Roberts also joked with AM 570 earlier this month. “Our dinosaurs have come through in the biggest spots.”
That was not always the case during the second half of this year’s regular season, when the Dodgers’ offense slipped into such a glaring funk –– highlighted by an inability to consistently slug the ball –– that one rival scout remarked in late August: “This is the oldest they’ve ever looked.”
Since then, however, they have rediscovered a jolt. They scored the fourth-most runs in the majors in September. They outslugged the Braves in the NLDS by belting eight home runs, all but one of which came from players age 33 or older.
Now, they are banking on their experience to give them an edge in this week’s NLCS, starting with a showdown against 24-year-old flamethrowing Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1 on Sunday.
“The toughest part about age is [managing it during the regular] season,” Roberts said. “But once you get through the marathon and you get to the sprint of the postseason, advantage goes to us in the sense of the experience.”
Father Time, of course, will eventually win out at some point.
Even Muncy acknowledged that there has been “some talk” of this being a potential final ride for this version of the roster.
“For us, it’s about playing for each other, and that’s what makes it so special,” Muncy said. “A lot of us have been through a lot of moments together –– good, bad, in the middle –– and I wouldn’t want to share those with anyone else, that’s for sure.”
For now, however, the Dinosaur Dodgers just want to keep on roaring.
Eight wins away from another World Series, age is the least of their concerns.
“I don’t like thinking that this could be towards the end [of our run], because I don’t think it is,” Muncy said. “I think we still have a lot of good baseball left in us. Hopefully we can keep going.”

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: He finally did it! Dodgers' Andy Pages ends two-year postseason slump at the perfect time
item.dc:creator: Bill Plaschke

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
He pounded his chest twice as he left the batter’s box, and all of Dodgers nation rocked to the beat.
Andy Pages did it. He finally did it. He finally broke out of his baffling two-year October slump with a hit so powerful, he didn’t even have to climb over Kiké Hernández to get it.
How powerful? With one smooth swing he broke a tie by scoring two runs while sending two teams packing, the Atlanta Braves trudging home for the winter and the Dodgers charging into the National League Championship Series.
Yeah, it was a blast, both figuratively and literally, Pages’ two-out, two-strike bases-loaded single in the seventh inning Wednesday night silencing the lame tomahawk-chopping fans at Truist Park and giving the Dodgers an eventual clinching 4-1 victory against the Braves in the National League Division Series.
Certainly, it only gets tougher from here. In winning this best-of-five series three games to one, the Dodgers can now prepare for a best-of-seven showdown task against either the mighty Milwaukee Brewers or blazing San Diego Padres.
Yes, they will need to hit better, they will need Blake Snell to find his focus, they will need Shohei Ohtani to show up.
But…Andy Pages! Seriously! If a guy who was seven for 66 in the last two postseasons and was so helpless last year he was benched for the last three games of the World Series…if that guy can drive in the winning run from the bottom of the order? The once-fallible Dodgers may just be unbeatable.
“There’s no more talented team than the Los Angeles Dodgers,” manager Dave Roberts shouted in the postgame clubhouse. “We’re the best organization in sports, top to bottom. We’re smarter, we’re better, and we’re tougher.”
At that point, someone referenced a recent comment from Padres owner José E. Feliciano insinuating that the Dodgers, baseball’s oldest team, was composed of dinosaurs.
“And we’re dinosaurs!” shouted a voice above the clubhouse din.
If they’re dinosaurs, their first initial is “T” and their last name is ‘Rex.”
It’s OK to start seriously thinking about a three-peat now. They’re now just eight wins away but, given how mediocre the American League playoff teams appear, they could realistically be just four wins away.
Andy Pages comes through in the seventh inning to break a tie and four relievers close out a 3-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves to win the NLDS in four games.
Here’s guessing that the NLCS will be the real World Series. And here’s guessing the Dodgers will be ready.
Pages, who won the hearts of Dodger fans last October when he made a leaping game-saving catch over the back of Kiké Hernández, was granted his first big October swing thanks to the Braves largess.
In the seventh inning of a 1-all tie, Teoscar Hernández redeemed himself for another fielding blunder with a single that finally drove dizzying Tyler Mahle from the game.
In came Game 2 rookie sensation Didier Fuentes, only this time, he was all rookie and zero sensation, walking Josue De Paula and Kyle Tucker to load the bases. Considering De Paula is just a kid and Tucker has been struggling, the fact that both showed such patience in such a pressure situation was pretty cool. And moments later, it got even cooler.
In came veteran reliever Robert Suarez, and Pages was ready for him, working the count full before lining the two-run single up the middle.
The Dodgers added a run two innings later on a Max Muncy home run — has there ever been a playoff game when he hasn’t homered? — to finalize the score.
When the game ended on an Austin Riley fly out to right field, Pages celebrated in center field by taking off his cap, turning his face to the sky and pounding the cap three times into his glove.
It was a series that was worth the emotion, the Dodgers famous starting rotation giving up just four runs in 21 ⅓ innings, the bullpen solid behind a revived Edwin Díaz, and the offense doing just enough to beat Braves aces Chris Sale and Mahle.
In the fifth inning of a tie game, starter Tyler Glasnow issued walks to Riley and Michael Harris II. With two out, in came Alex Vesia. Up stepped slugger Matt Olson. The fans climbed to their feet. This was the Braves’ big chance.
But Olson swung at the first pitch and lined it directly to second baseman Kiké Hernández to end the threat and quiet the joint. Díaz threw a hitless ninth for his second save of the series and…who’s going to beat them?
Afterward, Roberts referenced nearly half of his team when talking about his pride. He talked about Pages’ hit, about De Paula’s walk, about reliever Edgardo Henriquez’s 1 ⅔ shutout innings, about Muncy’s bat and Freddie Freeman’s glove
“I guess, amazement,” he said. “Our guys just continue to fight, persevere. You never know who the guy’s going to be.”
The only glaring weakness was, once again, the superstar who used to be their strength. Ohtani scored the Dodgers’ first run after drawing a walk but went hitless in three ensuing at-bats. He only got two hits in the four-game series and you have to wonder if his injury-wracked body would be better out of the lineup.
How well are they playing without the full services of their most historic player? On the verge of making history, the Dodgers don’t even miss him.
