item.content:encoded:
8 de octubre de 2026 - 9:55 PM
Atlanta - Andy Pages impulsó dos carreras con un sencillo con las bases llenas en la séptima entrada para darle la ventaja definitiva a Los Ángeles, y los reinante bicampeones Dodgers vencieron el miércoles 4-1 a los Braves de Atlanta para sentenciar su serie divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Los Dodgers ganaron juegos consecutivos en Atlanta para llevarse 3-1 la serie al mejor de cinco y avanzar a la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional dentro de empeño por convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional que conquista tres Series Mundiales seguidas.
El cubano Pages conectó una línea por el centro a un lanzamiento en cuenta de 3-2 del venezolano Robert Suárez para remolcar al dominicano Teoscar Hernández, quien había empalmado un sencillo ante el abridor Tyler Mahle, y al corredor emergente Tommy Edman, para poner el 3-1 en el marcador 3-1.
Acto seguido, el colombiano Didier Fuentes concedió base por bolas al bateador emergente dominicano Josue De Paula y a Kyle Tucker para congestionar las bases. Edman corrió por De Paula.
El jonrón solitario de Max Muncy ante el cubano Raisel Iglesias en la novena aumentó la ventaja y dejó al toletero con un gran total de 19 cuadrangulares de postemporada con los Dodgers, ampliando su récord de la franquicia.
El derecho de los Dodgers Tyler Glasnow, en su primera apertura desde el 24 de septiembre, permitió apenas un hit, pero otorgó cinco bases por bolas en cuatro innings y dos tercios.
Después de conceder dos boletos en la quinta, el zurdo Alex Vesia terminó la entrada con un rodado de Matt Olson a la segunda base.
La oportunidad desperdiciada dejó a los Braves con 18 pasaporte en la serie, pero ninguno se concretó en carrera.
Glasnow y cuatro relevistas se combinaron para permitir apenas tres hits. Tanner Scott lanzó una octava entrada perfecta antes de que el puertorriqueño Edwin “Sugar” Díaz sacara tres outs rápidos para apuntarse el salvamento.
Fue el segundo salvamento en noches consecutivas para Díaz, de vuelta en el puesto de cerrador de los Dodgers.
Mahle, originario de Newport Beach, California, y que creció como aficionado de los Dodgers, permitió dos carreras —una limpia— en seis innings y un tercio.
Michael Harris II conectó el primer lanzamiento de Glasnow para un sencillo antes de robarse la segunda y, finalmente, anotar desde tercera con un lanzamiento descontrolado que rebotó en el protector de pecho del receptor Will Smith.
Los Dodgers empataron en la segunda con ayuda de dos errores de Atlanta. Shohei Ohtani recibió base por bolas, se robó la segunda y avanzó a tercera por un tiro desviado del receptor Sean Murphy hacia el jardín central. El elevado de Muncy a la zona corta del jardín izquierdo fue dejado caer por el campocorto hondureño Mauricio Dubón para otro error, lo que permitió que Ohtani anotara.
Hernández se estrelló contra la pared al intentar atrapar el doble de Ozzie Albies ante Vesia para abrir la sexta. Hernández se señaló la cabeza y el cuello al hablar con un preparador físico, pero se mantuvo en el juego.
El venezolano Edgardo Henríquez dejó varado a Albies en segunda. Henríquez permitió un hit al cubrir una entrada y dos tercios sin carrera para llevarse la victoria.
Las noticias explicadas de forma sencilla y directa para entender lo más importante del día.

item.title: [New York Post] Doctober classic propels Dodgers to NLCS in quest for World Series three-peat
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: ATLANTA — Dave Roberts didn’t hesitate. So what if Tyler Glasnow had thrown only 78 pitches? So what if he was still in the fifth inning? Glasnow had walked his second batter of the inning, and Roberts wasn’t about to take any chances. Calling on Alex Vesia to record the final out of the inning, Roberts initiated a chaotic sequence of events that resulted in the Dodgers claiming a 4-1 victory over the Braves in Game 4 of their National League Division Series. The Dodgers advanced to the NL Champ
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Dave Roberts didn’t hesitate.
So what if Tyler Glasnow had thrown only 78 pitches?
So what if he was still in the fifth inning?
Glasnow had walked his second batter of the inning, and Roberts wasn’t about to take any chances.
Calling on Alex Vesia to record the final out of the inning, Roberts initiated a chaotic sequence of events that resulted in the Dodgers claiming a 4-1 victory over the Braves in Game 4 of their National League Division Series.
The Dodgers advanced to the NL Championship Series.
Because of Tarik Skubal.
Because of Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
Because of Freddie Freeman.
And because of David Ray Roberts, the manager affectionately known as Doc who has a game or two like this every October.
The victory over the Braves on Wednesday was a Doctober classic.
On a day in which one of his four aces lasted only 4 ⅔ innings, Roberts figured out how to cover 13 outs of the game with a notoriously unpredictable bullpen.
Roberts’ fingerprints were also all over Andy Pages’ two-run single in the seventh inning that broke open the game.
When Teoscar Hernandez singled that inning with one out, Braves manager Walt Weiss replaced starting pitcher Tyler Mahle with right-hander Didier Fuentes.
Fuentes forced Max Muncy to ground out, but Hernandez advanced to second base on the play.
Due up was Game 3 hero Kike Hernandez.
Rather than have the right-handed utilityman face Fuentes, Roberts deployed rookie Josue De Paula as a pinch hitter. The left-handed-hitting De Paula drew a walk, at which point he was replaced on the basepaths by Tommy Edman.
Kyle Tucker followed up with another walk to load the bases, at which point Weiss turned to fireballer Robert Suarez to pitch to Pages.
Pages batted .078 in the postseason last year, which resulted in his benching in the World Series. He was 0-for-7 in the first two games of this series, but Roberts stuck with him.
Roberts’ faith was rewarded by the most important hit of Pages’ three-year career, a single to right field that drove in two runs to push the Dodgers in front, 3-1. The runs were the Dodgers’ first of the series that weren’t scored via a home run.
The manager demonstrated an equal level of creativity in directing his bullpen.
Vesia returned for the sixth inning, only to give up a leadoff double to Ozzie Albies. Roberts kept the left-hander in for another batter, the left-handed-hitting Drake Baldwin, who lined out.
Roberts’ next call to the bullpen was for Edgardo Henriquez, who spent the last two weeks of the regular season on the injured list. Henriquez gave up a run in the Dodgers’ Game 2 loss, but not only did Roberts trust him to prevent Albies from scoring, he also had him pitch the seventh inning.
From there, it was simple.
Tanner Scott pitched the eighth inning. With Muncy homering in the ninth inning to increase the lead to 4-1, Edwin Diaz came in to record the last three outs.
The Dodgers moved to within four wins of playing in their third consecutive World Series, and they did it with Shohei Ohtani still missing in action.
Ohtani was 2-for-13 in this series.
“It’s good to know that we can still win games without him doing a whole bunch,” Roberts said. “But he’s going to come to life. It will happen.”
Roberts has squinted extra hard in recent days to find evidence of that.
Here’s the reality: In his last 22 combined games between the regular season and playoffs, Ohtani has no home runs and only one RBI.
That isn’t a slump.
The No. 1 player in the game doesn’t go this long without hitting in the prime of his career without something being seriously wrong with him.
Ohtani spent 15 days last month on the injured list because of a discomfort in his right arm. A couple of days before he was placed on the IL, he said his left knee was also bothering him.
The uncertainty over Ohtani’s capabilities forced Roberts to move him around the lineup.
With Mookie Betts grinding out quality at-bats as the leadoff hitter and Freeman producing enough to solidify his place as the team’s No. 2 hitter, Ohtani was removed from the top of the order.
Against the left-handed Chris Sale in Game 3, Ohtani batted fifth. Against the right-handed Mahle on Wednesday, he batted cleanup.
Ohtani managed to create something out of nothing in the second inning. He drew a walk, then stole second base, prompting Braves catcher Sean Murphy to airmail a throw into center field. Ohtani scampered to third base. When Braves shortstop Mauricio Dubón dropped a popup by Muncy in shallow left field, Ohtani scored to tie the game at 1.
Ohtani didn’t collect any hits Wednesday, but he didn’t have to.
Roberts had the game under control.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Andy Pages' clutch hit sends Dodgers past Braves, into NLCS
item.description: ATLANTA — Andy Pages’ two-run single in the seventh inning broke open a pitchers’ duel and helped the Los Angeles Dodgers close out their National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves with a 4-1 win in Game 4 on Wednesday. The Dodgers, who won the series 3-1 and are looking to be the first National League team to win three straight World Series, await the winner of the other NLDS between the Brewers and Padres. Milwaukee leads that best-of-five set 2-1 entering a Wednesday matchup i
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Andy Pages’ two-run single in the seventh inning broke open a pitchers’ duel and helped the Los Angeles Dodgers close out their National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves with a 4-1 win in Game 4 on Wednesday.
The Dodgers, who won the series 3-1 and are looking to be the first National League team to win three straight World Series, await the winner of the other NLDS between the Brewers and Padres. Milwaukee leads that best-of-five set 2-1 entering a Wednesday matchup in San Diego.
Pages’ hit was Los Angeles’ first with runners in scoring position in the series after the team started 0-for-14. It came off of Robert Suarez after Teoscar Hernandez hit a one-out single against Braves starter Tyler Mahle and then reliever Didier Fuentes issued back-to-back two-out walks.
Pages had two of the Dodgers’ five hits and two of their three RBIs in the win.
His clutch hit came the inning after Atlanta got nothing out of Ozzie Albies’ leadoff double, with Edgardo Henriquez (1-0) escaping the jam to earn his first career postseason victory.
Los Angeles’ Max Muncy tacked on an insurance run with a solo homer in the ninth, his third long ball of the postseason.
Mahle (0-1) was a tough-luck loser, charged with two runs (one earned) on three hits over 6 1/3 innings. He struck out four and walked one.
Michael Harris II had two of Atlanta’s three hits, including a double. However, the Braves’ situational hitting issues continued as they finished the series 1-for-23 with runners in scoring position.
Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow battled through 4 1/3 innings, allowing just one run on one hit, walking five and striking out five. Alex Vesia, Henriquez, Tanner Scott and Edwin Diaz followed and combined to allow no runs on two hits over the final 4 1/3 innings, setting down the final seven Atlanta batters in a row.
Diaz earned his second save of the series.
Los Angeles’ pitching staff gave up eight runs on 18 hits over the four-game series.
The Braves opened the scoring in the bottom of the first on a wild pitch that scored Harris. He led off with a single, stole second and moved to third on a fielder’s choice.
The Dodgers equalized in the second behind a pair of Braves errors. Shohei Ohtani drew a leadoff walk, stole second and moved to third on an errant throw from catcher Sean Murphy. Muncy then hit a sky-high popup to shallow left that shortstop Mauricio Dubon dropped, allowing Ohtani to score.
–Curt Weiler, Field Level Media

item.title: [Orange County Register] Andy Pages comes through in the clutch to send Dodgers to NLCS
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: ATLANTA — Overmatched last postseason and benched during the World Series, Andy Pages used the embarrassment to fuel an All-Star season in 2026. But he was hit by a pitch on Aug. 21 that broke a bone in his hand, didn’t return until the final six games of the regular season and started the postseason, trying to do too much (by his manager’s estimation) to make up for last fall’s lack of contributions. The accounts have been reconciled. It was Pages’ clutch two-out, two-run single in the seventh
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Overmatched last postseason and benched during the World Series, Andy Pages used the embarrassment to fuel an All-Star season in 2026.
But he was hit by a pitch on Aug. 21 that broke a bone in his hand, didn’t return until the final six games of the regular season and started the postseason, trying to do too much (by his manager’s estimation) to make up for last fall’s lack of contributions.
The accounts have been reconciled. It was Pages’ clutch two-out, two-run single in the seventh inning that broke a tie and lifted the Dodgers to a 4-1 victory on Wednesday night in Game 4 of their National League Division Series with the Atlanta Braves.
The victory sends the Dodgers to the National League Championship Series against either the Milwaukee Brewers or San Diego Padres. The Dodgers have reached baseball’s Final Four for the fifth time in the past seven years, the eighth time in the past 11. Their quest for a ‘three-peat’ will continue Sunday either in Milwaukee or at home against the Padres.
This series was decided in the seventh inning.
With the score tied 1-1, Teoscar Hernandez – fresh off a collision with the left field wall that left him on the warning track dirt, rubbing the left side of his head – singled with one out off Braves starter Tyler Mahle. It was just the third hit off Mahle and it came on just his 85th pitch. But Braves manager Walt Weiss went to his bullpen, bringing in Game 2 hero Didier Fuentes to face Max Muncy.
Fuentes got Muncy to ground out, Hernandez moving to second, but he walked pinch-hitter Josue De Paula and Kyle Tucker to load the bases with two outs.
Weiss had a quick hook, pulling Fuentes and handing the ball to veteran Robert Suarez to face Pages. Pages got ahead in the count, 3-and-1, then swung and missed at a 99.1 mph fastball from Suarez. He got another fastball on the full count and didn’t miss, stroking it through the middle for the Dodgers’ first – and only hit – with a runner in scoring position in their 16 at-bats in those situations during the four games of this series.
Runs had been hard to come by in Atlanta. After Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Chris Sale squared off in Game 3, Mahle and Tyler Glasnow allowed just a dirty run each through the first six innings.
In the bottom of the first, Michael Harris II led off with a single off of Glasnow. He stole second, went to third on a ground out and score when Glasnow spiked a knuckle curve in the dirt well in front of home plate. It bounced off Will Smith’s chest protector back towards the mound and Glasnow couldn’t retrieve it in time to get Harris.
In the top of the second, Shohei Ohtani took a five-pitch walk, stole second and went to third when Braves catcher Sean Murphy threw the ball into center field. Ohtani scored when Braves shortstop Mauricio Dubon dropped Max Muncy’s pop-up in shallow left field.
Mahle struck out only four in his 6⅓ innings (three of them consecutively in the fourth inning) and got just seven swings-and-misses on 95 pitches. But he got a lot of soft contact – and when he didn’t, it usually found a Braves fielder’s glove. The Dodgers hit seven balls in the first six innings with exit velocities of 95 mph or higher (the StatCast standard for “hard-hit”). Only one of them was a base hit – Pages’ third-inning single (106.7 mph).
Against Glasnow, the Braves just didn’t make much contact at all.
He gave up that leadoff single to Harris in the first inning but no other hits. He did walk five, though, including two in the fifth inning that prompted Manager Dave Roberts to pull him from the game after 78 pitches.
Dodgers pitchers somehow walked 18 batters in the series but let none of them score. Alex Vesia retired Matt Olson to end that fifth inning. Edgardo Henriquez held the Braves scoreless over the next two. Tanner Scott retired the slumping heart of the Braves’ order and Muncy gave Edwin Diaz cushion in the ninth inning with a solo home run (his 19th career postseason homer, a franchise record).
More to come on this story.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Andy Pages single beats Braves, Dodgers win NLDS in 4 games
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: It took until the seventh inning of the fourth game of the National League Division Series for the Dodgers to get their first hit with a runner in scoring position. But Andy Pages made it count, with a two-run single to break a tie in a 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves on Wednesday night at Truist Park, clinching the NLCS to send the Dodgers to their third National League Championship Series in a row. The winning rally started with a single by Teoscar Hernández, just minutes after crashing into t
item.content:encoded:
It took until the seventh inning of the fourth game of the National League Division Series for the Dodgers to get their first hit with a runner in scoring position. But Andy Pages made it count, with a two-run single to break a tie in a 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves on Wednesday night at Truist Park, clinching the NLCS to send the Dodgers to their third National League Championship Series in a row.
The winning rally started with a single by Teoscar Hernández, just minutes after crashing into the left field wall on a Braves double in the previous half-inning. That ended the night for Tyler Mahle, who continued to have the Dodgers number, once again pitching into the seventh.
In came Game 2 Braves hero Didier Fuentes, whose second batter faced was fellow 21-year-old pinch-hitter Josue De Paula, only 24 days his senior. De Paula, in just his second postseason plate appearance, walked, then was removed for pinch-runner Tommy Edman. Kyle Tucker also walked to load the bases, setting up Pages — the Dodgers RBI leader this season — to single home a pair.
After going hitless in his first two games this series, Pages had two hits in Game 3 and two more in Game 4, equaling his total for the entire postseason in 2025. The hit also snapped an 0-for-14 skid by the Dodgers with runners in scoring position to start this series.
The first of those runs snapped a string of 22 straight innings by Mahle against the Dodgers without allowing an earned run, dating all the way back to 2022.
Edgardo Henriquez, who entered with one out in the sixth inning and stranded a runner on second, followed with a scoreless seventh inning to bookend the Dodgers rally, and earned the win.
Just like in Game 3, Tanner Scott pitched a scoreless eighth and Edwin Díaz closed out the win in the ninth, giving the Dodgers the planned back end of their bullpen that hadn't really been fully intact since early April.
Dodgers pitchers allowed eight total runs in the four-game series.
Max power
Max Muncy added some insurance with a solo home run in the ninth inning, extending his Dodgers career postseason record with now 19 home runs. Muncy also homered in Games 1 and 2 of this series, matching his most prolific postseason series with the long ball. He also hit three home runs in the 2019 NLDS against the Washington Nationals.
Sloppy start
Both teams exchanged mistakes for each other's first run, including an errant throw into center field on a stolen base attempt from each side. Michael Harris II got a great jump from third base on a wild pitch by Tyler Glasnow that didn't get too far from home plate in the first inning, catching the Dodgers flat-footed. In the top of the second, Shohei Ohtani walked, stole second and went to third on the bad throw, then scored when a Max Muncy popup into short left field was biffed by shortstop Mauricio Dubón.
Glasnow improved a bit as the game progressed, and didn't allow another hit after Harris led off the game with a single. But, like Blake Snell in Game 2, Glasnow on Wednesday walked five batters, including two in the fifth inning — a leadoff free pass to Austin Riley after getting ahead 0-2, and a two-out, four-pitch walk to Ronald Acuña Jr. to end Glasnow's night early.
The Dodgers right-hander struck out five with those five walks in his 4 2/3 innings, and like Snell limited the damage to only one run. Alex Vesia helped, inducing a groundout to second base to end the fifth inning with those two Glasnow walks left stranded on base, and the game still tied.
Glasnow threw 78 pitches, 44 for strikes.
Not so free passes
None of Glasnow's five walks in Game 4 scored, and none of the 18 Braves who walked in the NLDS have touched home plate. But there have still been costs to that Dodgers wildness. For one, the Dodgers had to turn to its bullpen much earlier than hoped in two of the four games.
Also, two of Snell's walks in the first inning of Game 2, pushing Acuña to third base, which allowed him to score on an infield single. In Game 3, the pinch-hit walk by Rowdy Tellez pushed Dubón to third base, which allowed him to score on a groundout. So the walks have been costly, even if not as much as perhaps they should have been.
NLDS Game 4 particulars
Home run: Max Muncy (3)
WP — Edgardo Henriquez (1-0): 1 2/3 IP, 1 hit
LP — Tyler Mahle (0-1): 6 1/3 IP, 3 hits, 2 runs (1 earned), 1 walk, 4 strikeouts
Sv — Edwin Díaz (2): 1 IP, 1 strikeout
Up next
The Dodgers move on to a third consecutive National League Championship Series, and eighth in the last 11 years, beginning Sunday night (time TBD, Fox Sports) either in Milwaukee against the Brewers or at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles against the Padres.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Teoscar Hernández Believes Looks at Atlanta Bullpen Will Help
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers leave Los Angeles tied 1-1 in the NLDS, but Teoscar Hernández believes the first two games may still help them as the series shifts to Atlanta. The Braves have already shown the Dodgers a lot of their bullpen, and Hernández thinks that can matter when the same arms start showing up again in Games 3 and 4. With Chris Sale waiting for them Tuesday, the Dodgers will need every edge they can get. A Better Read on Atlanta’s Bullpen “I think so,” Hernández said when asked
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers leave Los Angeles tied 1-1 in the NLDS, but Teoscar Hernández believes the first two games may still help them as the series shifts to Atlanta.
The Braves have already shown the Dodgers a lot of their bullpen, and Hernández thinks that can matter when the same arms start showing up again in Games 3 and 4. With Chris Sale waiting for them Tuesday, the Dodgers will need every edge they can get.
A Better Read on Atlanta’s Bullpen
“I think so,” Hernández said when asked whether seeing so many Atlanta relievers could help later in the series. “Moving forward, now that we’ve seen basically the best out of the bullpen, we can have a better plan. We can make a better plan for Tuesday and Wednesday.”
Atlanta leaned heavily on its bullpen in Game 2 and found a way to hold the Dodgers to one run. Hernández said the Dodgers will take what they learned from those matchups and use it when they see those pitchers again.
He also brushed aside the idea that Sunday felt like a major missed chance because of the number of pitchers Atlanta had already used during the Wild Card round.
“Not really,” he said. “We didn’t think about it. We were just trying to make the best plan that we could get for the series and trying to execute whatever we have to do.”
Experience Matters Now
With the series down to three games, Hernández pointed to the Dodgers’ recent postseason experience as something they can draw on.
“I think it’s big,” he said. “We’ve been in tougher spots than this one. It’s a one-one series.
“We all know they’re going to have the best starting pitcher that they have in Sale. We’re just going to try to be ready, go with the best plan and try to execute it.”
The Dodgers will counter Sale with Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
“It’s good,” Hernández said. “That’s the best pitcher that we have going against the best pitcher that they have. It’s going to be a good matchup, a good game.
“Hopefully at the end of the day, we get the win.”
Getting the Offense Going
The Dodgers have relied almost entirely on home runs for their scoring through the first two games, and Hernández said the answer is tied to better at-bats and strike-zone control.
“It’s just having good at-bats, not swinging at bad pitches,” he said. “Like I was saying, they were executing really good pitches today. They didn’t give us a really good chance to score runs.”
Hernández felt the Dodgers stayed patient Sunday.
“Yeah, I feel so,” he said. “Like I said, they made some good pitches, borderline pitches. It’s one of those days.”
Even with runners reaching throughout the game, Hernández said the approach in the dugout stayed the same.
“Just go in there, fight every at-bat, every pitch, and try to get a good result at the end of the day.”
The Dodgers will get another look at Atlanta’s pitching Tuesday. This time, Sale will be the first challenge. After that, Hernández believes the familiarity gained over the first two games could start working in their favor.

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers are back in Atlanta for Game 4 of the NLDS on Wednesday, needing just one more win to clinch the series. After getting to Chris Sale in Game 3, the Dodgers will face right-hander Tyler Mahle, who has turned heads since being acquired at the trade deadline from the San Francisco Giants.
After batting fifth in the starting lineup for the first time as a Dodger, Shohei Ohtani will once again be hitting in the middle third of the order, this time moving up to the cleanup spot with Teoscar Hernández sliding down to the fifth spot in the order.
Max Muncy makes his first start this series since batting 8th in Game 1 against left-hander Dylan Dodd, this time batting sixth in the lineup with Miguel Rojas getting the day off after dealing with back tightness. The hero of Game 3 on offense, Kiké Hernández, makes his second straight start, this time batting seventh while getting the start at second base. Kyle Tucker once again hits in the 8 spot while Andy Pages rounds things out after a multi-hit performance.
Runs have been hard to come by so far this series, as the Dodgers have plated just 10 combined runs over their first three postseason games, all of which have come via home runs. The main Achilles heel for the Dodgers has been their consistent inability to produce with runners in scoring position, as the team is 0-13 in those situations. The Braves, to their credit, have managed to get one hit with runners in scoring position, albeit across 14 at-bats, and have combined to score just eight runs over the first three games.
The Dodgers have fared well in previous matchups against Mahle, as the right-hander has a combined 3-3 record with a 3.15 ERA. Most of the damage came when Mahle was still with the Cincinnati Reds, and in his most recent start against the Dodgers back when he was with San Francisco, he shut them down over seven shutout innings in a 3-0 Giants win on April 22. Since joining Atlanta, Mahle finished the regular season with a 1.99 ERA and limited the Philadelphia Phillies to just one run in his most recent Wild Card start.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are coming off a massive Game 3 victory over the Atlanta Braves on the road at Truist Park on Tuesday night.
They’ll now take a 2-1 series lead into Wednesday’s matchup and sit just one win away from advancing to the NLCS as they continue to chase a third consecutive World Series title.
Ahead of the matchup. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts elected to make some changes to his starting lineup for the second straight day.
Dodgers Announce Teoscar Hernandez Change
Among those moving in the order is slugger Teoscar Hernandez, who hit third in the lineup Tuesday and will now drop to sixth for Game 4.
Hernandez is coming off back-to-back 0-for-4 performances. And Roberts will move catcher Will Smith into the No. 3 spot, while Shohei Ohtani moves from fifth to fourth and will bat cleanup.
Max Muncy will bat fifth in the lineup after starting Tuesday’s game on the bench.

Looking at the Dodgers
L.A. has relied heavily on the long ball for its offense so far in this series against Atlanta.
After winning 5-3 in Game 1, losing 3-2 in Game 2 on Sunday and then winning 3-1 on Tuesday, all 10 of their combined runs in the series have come via home runs.
And they’ve seemingly done it with Shohei Ohtani being pretty much a non-factor at the plate.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Dodgers beat Braves on Kiké Hernández and Freddie Freeman homers, take 2-1 NLDS lead

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
ATLANTA — The Dodgers went into Game 3 of the National League Division Series knowing they couldn’t be so reliant on the home run, especially with Braves ace Chris Sale on the mound. And yet, in a 3-1 win, it was the home run ball, paired with a masterful performance on the mound from right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, that secured the victory.
The Dodgers pulled ahead to a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five series.
The Dodgers tried to score in other ways, putting on six baserunners in the first three innings of the game. But it didn’t work.
They failed to take advantage of some luck and poor defense from the Braves in the first inning, as Mookie Betts beat out a soft ground ball up the first base line and Teoscar Hernández reached on a fielding error by Braves shortstop Ha-Seong Kim.
Yoshinobu gives up four hits and strikes out 10 and Kiké Hernández hits a two-run home run to power the Dodgers to victory in Game 3 of the NLDS.
The lineup shuffling manager Dave Roberts did against Sale had superstar Shohei Ohtani, batting fifth, walking up to the plate with two outs and runners on first and second. His over-anxious approach at the plate so far this postseason followed him into the at-bat. And he struck out whiffing on a slider in the opposite batter’s box.
The next inning, Kyle Tucker hit a two-out single into left, baited Sale into picking over to first base twice, and then stole second. But he was stranded there, as Kiké Hernández went down swinging. All six of the Dodgers’ outs in the first two innings came via the strikeout.
In the third, the Dodgers loaded the bases. Mookie Betts started the effort with a double through the left side of the infield. And it looked for a moment as if Freddie Freeman had capitalized on the opportunity with a runner in scoring position.
He stayed back on a fastball and crushed it to deep left field, on a trajectory to just clear the short fence. But Braves left fielder Mauricio Dubón made a leaping catch, holding into the ball as he slammed into the wall.
Undeterred, the Dodgers kept putting runners on base. With two outs, Will Smith stayed through a slider to single. Ohtani clipped Braves catcher Drake Baldwin’s mitt and was awarded first base for catcher’s interference. Then Miguel Rojas, who’d exit the game in the eighth inning mid-at-bat with what the Dodgers called low back pain, hit a line drive that found leather to end the inning.
So, back to the long ball.
Perennial postseason hero Kiké Hernández delivered the first blow. With Andy Pages on first, after his first hit of the series, Hernández launched a changeup into the left-field stands. Then, two batters later, Freeman turned on an inside sinker and sent it over the right-field fence — where Dubón had no chance to track it down.
Game 3 was billed as a matchup between aces: Sale, whom the Braves tabbed for Tuesday because of his workload in their wild-card series, and Yamamoto, whom the Dodgers partially held back for the first two games with the NLCS in mind.
Yamamoto held up his end of the bargain, limiting the Braves to four hits and one run in seven innings.
He retired 10 of the first 11 batters he faced. The only baserunner in that time, Michael Harris II, bunted for a single. Yamamoto crashed hard, slipping on the slick grass as he tried to pivot but still managing to make a throw to first from the ground.
Shohei Ohtani is batting fifth in the lineup against Braves ace Chris Sale in Game 3 of the NLDS. He hasn’t hit fifth or lower in a starting lineup since 2020 with the Angels.
He only wavered in the fifth, loading the bases with a pair of singles and a four-pitch walk. The Braves’ batting order turned over, and Yamamoto got Baldwin to ground out to first, but that allowed a run. Then he induced Ronald Acuña Jr. to ground out to second to escape the jam. Rojas ranged to his left to field the ball and made an on-target throw even as he slipped on the grass in shallow right field.
Yamamoto didn’t allow another baserunner.
Left-handed reliever Tanner Scott served as the Dodgers’ setup man, throwing a hitless eighth. And right-hander Edwin Díaz came in for his first save opportunity since Aug. 14 against the Brewers.
He gave up a double off the wall to Ozzie Albies to open the inning but retired the next three batters.

item.title: [New York Post] Dave Roberts proves he’s a playoff wizard again as Dodgers erupt in 4th inning against Braves

But Hernandez needed to show off his bat first. Hernández saw an 89 MPH changeup come his way by Br
item.content:encoded:
Freddie Freeman and Kiké Hernández continue to add to their postseason résumés.
An inning after Freeman was denied an opposite-field home run over the left field wall at Truist Park by Mauricio Dubón, he thought he might try hitting one right.
But Hernandez needed to show off his bat first.
The two got the Dodgers on the board, to give them a 3-0 lead in the fourth inning of the NLDS, by hitting home runs over the walls in left and right field.
Hernández saw an 89 MPH changeup come his way by Braves starting pitcher Chris Sale and sent it 406 feet out of the park for a two-run homer. One batter later, Freeman obliterated a 96 MPH sinker and sent it screaming off the bat at 103 MPH for 399 feet.
Sale managed to get out of the inning in the following at-bat, but at first glance, it looked he was going to gve up another homer.
Teoscar Hernández just came short of Sale’s slider out of the park, after hard-hitting Sale at 108 MPH.
Both Freeman and Hernandez, continue to show why they are dominant in October, as both of them have had playoff heroics.
Freeman has a career batting average of .268 with 82 hits, 17 home runs, and 40 RBI through 81 postseason games.
Kiké Hernández has a career average of .272 with 80 hits and 16 home runs, with 42 RBIs in the postseason.
The combination of Hernández and Freeman came on the same day; manager Dave Roberts made a surprising decision to bump four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani down to the fifth hole in the Dodgers lineup and have Freeman hitting second, behind Mookie Betts, while Hernández was hitting ninth.
So far, his decision is paying off as Los Angeles holds a 3-1 lead against the Braves.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are tied with the Atlanta Braves at one game apiece in their best-of-five series in the NLDS.
On Tuesday night, the two teams will meet for Game 3 at Truist Park in Atlanta, with the Braves sending out left-handed ace Chris Sale while L.A. will start right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto in what should be one of the best pitching matchups we’ve seen so far this postseason.
Ahead of the game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made some major lineup changes, including one involving veteran slugger Freddie Freeman.
Dodgers Announce Freeman Move
With Shohei Ohtani struggling at the plate recently, Roberts decided to move him down to the No. 5 spot in the lineup Tuesday night.
As a result, Freeman will move up from the cleanup spot to the No. 2 spot, while Mookie Betts remains in the leadoff spot.
Teoscar Hernandez and Will Smith will fill the No. 3 and No. 4 spots, while the back end of the order will remain fairly close to what the Dodgers have used recently, despite bringing Andy Pages back into the lineup.

Freeman’s 2026 Postseason
While it’s only been two games, Freeman has been one of the most consistent bats in the Dodgers’ lineup against his former team.
He’s recorded three hits across seven at-bats, including two on Sunday, one of which was a home run.
Freeman spent the first 12 years of his MLB career with the Braves and became one of the greatest players in franchise history. Now, he’ll play the next two games in a ballpark he called home for more than a decade.

After hitting second in the first two games of the series, Ohtani was dropped to fifth ahead of Game 3 on Tuesday. Per The Athletic's Fabi
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are pushing two-way star Shohei Ohtani to fifth in the batting order following a tepid start to the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
After hitting second in the first two games of the series, Ohtani was dropped to fifth ahead of Game 3 on Tuesday. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Teoscar Hernández and Will Smith will hit ahead of Ohtani in Game 3.
In the two previous games in the series, Betts led off and Ohtani hit second.
Per The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya, Dodgers managers Dave Roberts told reporters that the move to fifth would be just for Tuesday's game against Braves ace Chris Sale. A lefty, Sale has been notoriously tough against left-handed batters over his career.
Roberts added that when he approached Ohtani about moving down in the order on Monday, Ohtani responded that he'd considered suggesting doing so in September as he struggled through injuries.
Hitting fifth is unusual for Ohtani, who hasn't hit that low since 2020, when he was a member of the Los Angeles Angels.
Ohtani hasn't been terrible in the first two games of the series, going 2-for-8 with two strikeouts. But other members of the team have outperformed the slugger in the NLDS. Freeman and Hernández, in particular, have ignited the Dodgers' offense. Smith, however, is hitless in eight at-bats thus far.
At the plate, Ohtani has been worse against lefties over his career, though he still has an excellent .853 OPS against them. That's actually higher than Smith's career OPS against left-handers.
Ohtani, however, came into the playoffs battling multiple injuries. On Friday, he acknowledged that left knee and right biceps issues will impact him throughout the postseason. Those same issues seemed to affect Ohtani in the second half, as he hit .241/.322/.472 in August before collapsing with a .200/.300/.233 line in eight games in September. At that point, the team put Ohtani on the injured list to give him time to recover for the playoffs.
Now that the playoffs are here, the Dodgers will try to ease Ohtani into a bigger role. While he hit second in the order early in the NLDS, a combination of his performance and Sale's presence on the mound will drop Ohtani much lower than he has hit in recent seasons.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Mookie Betts Isn't Crowing about the Dodgers' 100-Win Season
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO, CA — The Dodgers finished the regular season with 100 victories, but Mookie Betts already has his attention firmly fixed on October. Speaking with reporters following Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants, Betts discussed how he plans to maintain his recent offensive surge during the Dodgers’ five-day break, the importance of team chemistry, and the change in intensity that comes with postseason baseball. While Freddie Freeman and Teoscar Hernández expressed appreciation for reachi
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO, CA — The Dodgers finished the regular season with 100 victories, but Mookie Betts already has his attention firmly fixed on October.
Speaking with reporters following Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants, Betts discussed how he plans to maintain his recent offensive surge during the Dodgers’ five-day break, the importance of team chemistry, and the change in intensity that comes with postseason baseball.
While Freddie Freeman and Teoscar Hernández expressed appreciation for reaching the 100-win milestone, Betts offered a characteristically understated assessment.
A Hundred Wins? That’s Nice.
Asked whether another 100-win season carried particular significance for him and the team, Betts wasn’t especially sentimental.
“No, I don’t think so. Unless it’s some type of record or something. Not that I’m aware of. So, it means we played pretty good.”
For Betts, the more immediate concern is preserving the rhythm he established during a terrific September. The Dodgers’ shortstop has been one of the club’s hottest hitters over the final month, but maintaining that feel without regular games presents a challenge.
“I’m not sure. I don’t know if you can, just because games are kind of how you develop the rhythm,” he explained.
“But we’ll have the intrasquad games, and I’ve been in the league, what, 13 years now? So I’ll figure it out.”
Coming Together for Another October Run
The Dodgers successfully navigated a similar five-day break in 2024, using that time to prepare for the postseason while strengthening the team’s connection away from the field.
Betts believes that experience contributed to their championship run and expects the club to follow a similar approach this year.
“Yeah, I would say so. And I think we’re going to do it again. You know, I think this is the time where you really have to come together.
“There’s going to be a lot of adversity and whatnot. But it’s something that we’ve all been doing together for a while, and we get an opportunity to do it again.”
Asked whether his businesslike approach helps establish the team’s attitude heading into October, Betts said the entire clubhouse understands what lies ahead.
“Yeah, I would say so. But I think everybody has the same attitude. I think everybody, once we get to this time, we’ll be ready to go.
“And we understand that there is a distinct difference between now and the regular season. But, I mean, you obviously got to play the regular season.
“So now, getting to the postseason, we’ll keep the same attitude, but probably add a little more intensity and whatnot because it’s a short amount of time.”
September Momentum Is No Guarantee
The Dodgers’ offense enjoyed an excellent September, with Betts among the players finding their stride at precisely the right time. But when asked whether that momentum can carry into the playoffs, he offered a refreshingly straightforward answer.
“No idea.”
Betts elaborated that the quality of pitching changes considerably once the postseason begins, making it difficult to predict whether a team’s offensive success will continue.
“Yeah, I mean, you’re facing all the best pitching. Momentum is a thing, obviously, and so you never know. You never know what’s going to happen, and you can’t predict it.
“So you just got to go be ready.”
For Betts and the Dodgers, that preparation begins now. They’ll spend the next five days working through intrasquad games, maintaining their timing, and preparing for the winner of the Phillies-Braves Wild Card Series.
And when Saturday arrives, Betts expects the Dodgers to bring the same collective approach that helped carry them to last year’s championship, with a little extra October intensity thrown in.

Every subsequent trip to the plate, however, has been anything but. Granted, Ohtani has not been the Dodgers’ biggest problem offensively. Will
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers heroes, zeros from Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani still looks off
Heroes, zeros and the inside pitch from the Dodgers’ 3–2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in Game 2 of the National League Division Series:
Zero
Shohei Ohtani’s first at-bat of this NLDS looked relatively normal, as he pulled a 105 mph line drive into right for a first-inning, Game 1 single.
Every subsequent trip to the plate, however, has been anything but.
Granted, Ohtani has not been the Dodgers’ biggest problem offensively. Will Smith (0–for–8), Andy Pages (0–for–7, one walk) and Tommy Edman (0–for–5, one walk) are all vying for that honor.
But if there was any hope that the team’s playoff-opening bye week would fix the two-way amid his ongoing right arm and left knee injuries, these two games have been a reminder of just how far he is from his typical self.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine,” manager Dave Roberts said.
But…
“I don’t know if he’s trying to do too much because he doesn’t feel perfect,” the skipper added, in what felt more like a tacit acknowledgement.
A healthy Ohtani, after all, wouldn’t go 0–for–2 against plucky feel-good story Ray Kerr, striking out on an inside fastball in the first inning before popping out in a key spot with two aboard in the third.
A healthy Ohtani wouldn’t need to slap the ball the other way Ichiro-style just to get a base hit, as he did on his lone single in the fifth.
The most telling thing for the 32-year-old superstar the last two days?
The Braves haven’t been afraid to challenge him, throwing him nine fastballs in the middle-third of the strike zone so far. And he hasn’t been able to punish them for it, turning only one into a hit (that first-inning, Game 1 single) while also chasing more outside of the zone after failing to end his at-bats.
“He’ll be in there Game 3,” Roberts confirmed. “We’ve just got to, again, take good at-bats and expect the best.”
Hero
At least the Dodgers’ other pre-NLDS injury question mark has seemingly turned a corner.
In his final 66 games of the regular season (going back to July 5), Freddie Freeman had hit only one home run. In September, he slumped to a .184 average with only one extra-base hit while battling a right knee injury that threatened to linger into the playoffs.
However, the bye week seemingly did wonders for him, following up a one-hit, one-walk performance in Game 1 of the series with a two-hit night Sunday that included a solo homer to right field.
“I feel good, so I think we can be done with those questions,” he quipped when asked about his swing and knee injury. “Just more consistently getting myself in a good spot, being able to put good swings on it.”
Unsung hero
There were times this year when Edwin Díaz’s fastball velocity dipped as low as 92 mph.
During his scoreless appearance in the sixth inning on Sunday, the resurgent right-hander dialed it up to a season-high 100.8 mph.
That was just one impressive aspect of Díaz’s latest standout performance, in which he extended his scoreless streak to six innings (including 15 straight batters retired over his last five outings) since returning from his second injured list stint of the year on Sept. 18.
“Edwin was great,” Roberts said. “I think if you look at tonight, try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining and certainly a positive.”
Key stat
Zero: As in 0 hits with runners in scoring position for the Dodgers on Sunday, and 0 runs scored via any method other than a home run so far in this NLDS.
Ironically, the club’s lack of power had been the bigger concern coming into the playoffs.
While they could be (extremely) up-and-down in the regular season in situational at-bats, they still rank seventh in batting average with runners in scoring position and third in OPS.
That, however, hasn’t translated to October yet.
“Got to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” Freeman said. “I think that’s our biggest thing right now.”
Quote of the night
“We’ve been in tougher spots than this one,” outfielder Teoscar Hernández said, when asked how crucial the team’s past October experience (especially in back-and-forth series like the 2024 NLDS and 2025 World Series) would be in the face of what is now a best-of-three showdown. “It’s a 1–1 series. We know they’re going to have the best pitcher that they have, starting pitcher, in [Game 3 with Chris] Sale. But we’re just gonna try to be ready and just go with the best plan and just try to execute it.”

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The Dodgers placed super-utility man Enrique Hernandez on the injured list Wednesday and will do the same with left fielderTeoscar Hernandez the next time they play Friday.
Enrique Hernandez suffered what Dodgers manager Dave Roberts described as a "significant tear" in his oblique earlier this week, an injury that will keep him out for several weeks, if not months. Teoscar Hernandez pulled up lame while running to first base in Wednesday's second inning and was diagnosed with a left hamstring strain, though the initial expectation is that his injury is not as serious.
"He tested well," Roberts said after the Dodgers' 4-1 win over the Colorado Rockies. "But we're going to get a scan tomorrow. Obviously it's an IL. There's just no timeline. But something like that obviously is going to be a few weeks at the minimum."
Enrique Hernandez spent the season's first two months building back up after offseason elbow surgery and suffered the oblique injury while taking batting practice before his season debut Monday. He picked up two hits that night, received treatment Tuesday, homered, then hit a fourth-inning double under significant pain in his left side and was later replaced on defense.
Cameras caught Roberts consoling a visibly shaken Enrique Hernandez in the dugout shortly thereafter.
"I feel pretty defeated right now," Hernandez told reporters after the game.
The Dodgers recalled infield prospect Alex Freeland to fill the vacant roster spot, starting him at second base for the series finale. Freeland will probably get most of the playing time there until Tommy Edman makes his expected return from offseason ankle surgery at some point in June, though Hyeseong Kim will draw starts at second base, too.
The hope is that Enrique Hernandez will at least return for the stretch run of the regular season so he can be a factor in the playoffs, the time of year in which he usually shines. Teoscar Hernandez's stay should be shorter, though it's nonetheless painful for the Dodgers, given his 1.018 OPS over the past 18 games.
"It's pretty frustrating for us," Dodgers center fielder Andy Pages said in Spanish. "We have the opportunity to see them work hard every day and prepare so that those things don't happen. But [injuries are] going to happen all the time."

item.title: [True Blue LA] Dodgers NLDS notes: Blake Snell, Freddie Freeman, Didier Fuentes
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers and Braves shift their National League Division Series to Atlanta, tied at one game apiece. On the off day Monday, let’s look back a little more at the disappointing Game 2 loss by Los Angeles.
Blake Snell got only 11 outs on 90 pitches, and though he only allowed one run, the Dodgers used six relievers to cover the final 5 1/3 innings on Sunday. The Dodgers felt it was more rust than any lingering effects from the left groin discomfort that caused Snell to leave his start early on September 16 in Cincinnati.
“He just was fighting himself with his delivery all game,” Roberts said. “I think, in total, didn’t have fastball command, didn’t have slider command and the changeup wasn’t there. … It wasn’t the groin. He just wasn’t sharp tonight.”
All five runs the Dodgers scored in Game 1 came on home runs — two-run shots by Teoscar Hernández and Kyle Tucker, plus a solo shot by Mac Muncy. Then in Game 2 the Dodgers’ only two runs were on solo home runs from Freddie Freeman and Muncy. From Kevin Baxter of the Los Angeles Times:
“We’ve to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” added Freddie Freeman, who homered Sunday and has three hits in the series. “That’s our biggest thing right now. So keep getting guys on base and get that big hit.”
Freeman said the Braves have done a good job keeping the Dodger hitters off-balance by emptying their bullpen, sending in a fresh pitcher every couple of innings.
“It’s tough because you’re facing a different arm every single time you’re going up there,” Freeman said. “It’s different angles, different velocities, different things. So stringing hits together is very hard.
More from Roberts on Braves reliever Didier Fuentes, who retired 11 straight batters before Muncy homered in the ninth to pull the Dodgers within a run , from Bill Plunkett of the Orange County Register:
“I think it was just the fastball,” Roberts said of Fuentes, who threw two scoreless innings against the Dodgers during the Braves’ three-game sweep in Atlanta in August. “Tonight you could see the fastball, it was 99, 100. There was a lot of balls we were just missing as far as lazy fly balls, and we just couldn’t hit the ball flat against him. Then he was mixing in his split once in a while.
“Tip my hat to him, two days off (since pitching in the Wild Card Series) and doing what he did was pretty impressive.”

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — With the end of the regular season on Sunday, the statisticians can finally put down their pencils. We had a near miss for the triple crown in the American League (Yordan Alvarez) and a pitcher with a sub-2.00 ERA in the National League (Jacob Misiorowski). And though no Dodgers were at the top of any statistically categories this year, there were plenty featured in the NL Top Ten. Let’s do a quick end-of-season rundown, shall we?
The plan for two-way dominance Cy Young/MVP consideration sort of flamed out before the All-Star break, and Shohei was struggling to find his footing at the plate in the aftermath of a couple of injuries (most notably his right knee). However, even a diminished Ohtani is among the league’s elite and Shohei did enough in the first half of the season to lock down some Top-Ten finishes. He was tied for ninth in home runs with 30, tied for tenth in walks with 81, and 19th in batting average with .275. His other numbers were also top-ten-worthy: he finished sixth in the NL in On-Base Percentage with .377 and fifth in slugging percentage with .512. And, finally, his OPS of .889 was more than 100 lower than last year, but still third in the league behind Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong and the Nationals’ James Wood.
It was good year. But considering the wow factor of the first two years, a bit of a disappointment. Hopefully, he can get right in time to do damage like the old Shohei in the playoffs.
Despite his mighty struggles in September, Freddie turned in another strong campaign in 2026. Although his power number were down considerably, he still found his way on base at a clip not often seen in the modern game. Though his .288 batting average represented a low in Freddie’s Dodger years, it was still good enough for tenth place in the league. And, his 167 hits put him in eighth place in that category.
For those of you keeping track, he now stands at 2,598 hits in his career, 402 shy of the 3,000 mark that he’s had on his mind for a while. He’ll probably need three more years in the big league to reach that plateau, so that means the Dodgers would have to re-sign him after his current contract expires at the end of next year. Will that happen? It should, but I don’t know if Andrew Friedman wants to be sentimental about such things.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto was the only Dodger pitcher who logged enough innings to qualify for postseason awards, and he’s sure to get at least a sniff or two in the Cy Young voting. His year was probably his best yet: Fifth in wins (14), 3rd in ERA (2.53), 4th in innings pitched (185), 10th in strikeouts (182), 2nd in WHIP, and 2nd in Average Against (.182). Of course, all the hardwares going to the Miz this year, but Yamamoto’s steadiness is something to behold even if he doesn’t light up the radar gun on every pitch.
After a horrible year in 2025, no one was quite sure what to expect from Tanner Scott in 2026, and when Edwin Diaz went out with injury, there were more than a few Dodger fans who dreaded the thought of last year’s goat closing out games. However, Scott proved more than up to the task, converting 25 of 29 save opportunities, which put him in sixth place in the NL leader board. It will be interesting to see what happens as a resurgent Edwin Diaz seems to be ready for a return to the closer’s role.
Honorable mention….
Though they didn’t make any top tens, we should give it for Max Muncy, who made the All-Star team and finished 13th in the league in OPS and tied for 14th in the NL for homers. A really solid season from Max. Alex Vesia finished 7th in the league in appearances, and had an impact on more games than you might think. And, though they’re nowhere on the leaderboard, the strong finishes for Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez, and Kyle Tucker gives one hope for the postseason.
What about the team?
Since the Dodgers won the second most games in baseball, it only figures that they’d have a lot of nice numbers at the end of the year. On the hitting side, they finished fourth in home runs (204), fourth in RBI (756), 3rd in batting average (.257), second in slugging percentage (.424), and second in OPS (.762).
On the pitching side, they finished second in team ERA (3.55), 3rd in strikeouts (1,521), first in WHIP (1.18), and first in average against (.218). When you isolate the starters, the numbers are even better: first place in ERA, WHIP, and average against, and second in strikeouts.
The bullpen was good, but closer to the middle of the pack in the NL: fourth in ERA, fourth in saves, and fourth in WHIP. One stat that may work in the pen’s favor though: they finished 14th out of 15 NL teams in bullpen innings pitched. That means that other pens (save the Phillies) have been taxed more than the Dodgers. That could make a difference the deeper we go into October.
Conclusion
The numbers show kind of how 2026 felt: it was a good year, but not a dominant year. Many players, while still contributing, were down from their historical norms. And if the past is prologue, look for a lot of low-scoring games this October. Games that might be decided by one swing of the bat or one shut-down inning.
In the meantime, we wait. We watch and we wait.
See you Saturday!
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
Now that the 2026 MLB regular season is done, Sony made one last ratings tweak for many of the players across the league on October 2. The October MLB The Show 26 ratings update saw Mookie Betts & Cade Smith rise to join the other Diamonds in the game.
The notable changes
Mookie Betts is back as a Diamond in MLB The Show 26. He and Cade Smith were the only two to move to Diamond status on October 2. Betts moved to 85 OVR after a strong final few weeks. Over his last 14 games, Betts slashed .316/.418/.632 with four home runs and 10 extra-base hits.
Smith, meanwhile, notched 41 saves and struck out 107 batters over 74 innings this season for the Guardians.
Fernando Tatis Jr. moved up three points between the last update and now. Tatis Jr., before the start of the playoffs, hit five home runs and nine extra-base hits in the last 15 games of the regular season for San Diego.
Elly De La Cruz, who had eight extra-base hits in the final two weeks, moved to 87 OVR, a +2 OVR increase. He moved there, along with NL Wild Card hero Michael Harris II.
As for who went down, Yandy Diaz and Jacob deGrom were both downgraded from Diamond status.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula, bench shuffle
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA. One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered. Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

item.title: [si.com] The Potentially Fatal Flaw For Each MLB Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early. With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team. Brewers: Lack of Power The Brewers were baseball’s best team
item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.
